messages.text: I make $1,770 a month working at a call center. I live by myself. Do I qualify for SNAP?

**Short answer: you might. Your income is close to the line, so I'd encourage you to apply.** This is a rough first look, not a decision. Only the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS) can decide.

**Why it's close**
- **Income limit before deductions:** For a one-person household, the federal limit is $1,729 a month from Oct. 1, 2026 ([News4Jax, reporting USDA's 2027 limits](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)). Your $1,770 is about $41 over that.
- **Tennessee may use a higher limit:** News reports say Tennessee has moved to 200% of the poverty level. That would be roughly $2,600 or more for one person. But the sources I found disagree on whether this is in effect, and I couldn't confirm it on an official Tennessee page. So the result is **possibly**. It's worth applying either way.
- **Income after deductions:** SNAP also checks income after deductions. I took 20% off your wages and the $217 standard deduction ([News4Jax](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)). That leaves about $1,199 a month. That is under the $1,330 limit for one person, which I only found in a search summary and couldn't check on an official page.

**Benefit amount (estimate only)**
The most a one-person household can get is about $306 a month, according to news reports. I couldn't open the official USDA memo, so please treat that as unconfirmed. With no housing costs counted, your benefit would likely be $0. Rent and utility costs can lower your countable income and raise the amount.

**Two questions so I can estimate better:**
1. How much is your rent or mortgage each month? Do you pay for heating or cooling separately, or other utilities, or only a phone?
2. Are you 60 or older, or do you have a disability? (If so, different income rules apply.)

**How to apply**
- Online: [One DHS Customer Portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp)
- Phone: 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711), per [TDHS's SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
- Free local help: call 211

Please report your income and household accurately on the application. Overpayments have to be paid back.

Sources:
- [News4Jax: SNAP benefits increase](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)
- [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
rent is $800. i pay electric separately, and that covers heating and cooling. no other bills i can think of. i'm 33 and not disabled.

Rent and electric help. Here's my estimate.

**Your result: possibly.** I'd apply.

**The gross income test is still the open question.**
- Your income before deductions is $1,770. The 130% federal limit for one person is $1,729 ([News4Jax, reporting USDA's FY2027 numbers](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)).
- If Tennessee uses the reported 200% limit, you'd pass. I still couldn't confirm that on an official page. TDHS can tell you which limit applies.

**If you pass that test, here's the math (all estimates):**
- Your income after the 20% work deduction and the $217 standard deduction is about $1,199.
- Rent plus a utility allowance for electric heating and cooling can lower that a lot. Housing costs above half of your adjusted income count as an extra deduction. The cap on that deduction is $769 ([News4Jax](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)). Your $800 rent alone gives you about $200 of it, and the utility allowance adds more.
- I couldn't find Tennessee's current utility allowance amount, so I can't give an exact number.
- **My rough estimate is about $25 to $150 a month.** The lower end is if the utility allowance is small. The higher end is if it's large. This is a guess, not a promise.
- The most a one-person household can get is about $306 a month, and the minimum is $25. Both come from news reports, not the official USDA memo, which I couldn't open.

**Other things to know:**
- **Work rules:** Adults 18 to 64 without a disability or children are often expected to work or be in training about 20 hours a week. I haven't confirmed Tennessee's current rules. A caseworker can check this.
- **Savings:** Tennessee may count savings. The older limit was $3,000, but reports say that may have changed. Do you have more than about $3,000 in savings? You don't have to answer. It helps me tell you whether it could matter.

**How to apply**
- Online: [One DHS Customer Portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp)
- Phone: 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711), per [TDHS](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
- Free local help: call 211

Have your pay stubs, lease, and electric bill ready. Only TDHS can decide, and you can still apply even if the result looks unlikely.

Sources:
- [News4Jax: SNAP benefits increase](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)
- [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)
No, I've got about $300 in savings.

Thanks. $300 in savings is well under the older $3,000 limit I found, so savings shouldn't get in your way.

**Where you stand: possibly.**
- **Income after deductions:** It looks like you'd pass. Your adjusted income is about $1,199, and the limit is $1,330.
- **Income before deductions:** This is still the one open question. You're at $1,770, which is $41 over the 130% limit of $1,729 ([News4Jax, reporting USDA's FY2027 numbers](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)). If Tennessee uses the reported 200% limit, you'd pass. I couldn't confirm that on an official page.
- **Estimated benefit:** About $25 to $150 a month. This is a rough estimate. Tennessee's exact utility allowance would narrow it.

**What I'd do next**
1. Apply online at the [One DHS Customer Portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp). You can also call 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711), per [TDHS](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html).
2. Have your recent pay stubs, your lease, and an electric bill handy.
3. If you want help with the application, call 211 for free local help.

Applying costs nothing. A caseworker will check the current income limit and work rules, and only TDHS can decide.

Please report your income and rent exactly as they are. That protects you from having to pay back an overpayment later.

Do you want me to check whether you might also qualify for health coverage through TennCare?

Sources:
- [News4Jax: SNAP benefits increase](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)
- [TDHS SNAP page](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html)

For FY 2027 (October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2027), the 48 states, D.C., Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands use these one-person figures:

- **Gross monthly income limit: $1,729**, up from $1,696. The USDA memo sets this at 130 percent of poverty. This memorandum provides the fiscal year (FY) 2027 Cost-of-Living Adjustments for the program, effective as of October 1, 2026.
- **Net monthly income limit: $1,330**, which the USDA table lists at 100 percent of poverty. Gross income generally refers to a household's income before deductions, while net income is what remains after allowable deductions.
- **Standard deduction: $217** for household sizes one to three, up from $209. The maximum excess shelter deduction will increase from $744 to $796. Cronista reports that same cap as $789, so check the USDA table, which I did not see in full.

Alaska, Hawaii, Guam, and the Virgin Islands have separate tables. Alaska's one-person gross limit is $2,162 and Hawaii's is $1,989, per the USDA memo's figures. Elderly and disabled households that qualify as separate households use a different standard: 165% of the poverty level, which is $2,195 per month for one person in the 48 states according to News4Jax.

Tennessee appears to have moved to broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), which raises the gross income limit to 200% of the poverty line. The sources conflict on whether that change is in effect, so confirm with TDHS before relying on it.

- **Recent change (June 2026 reporting):** The Tennessee Department of Human Services has adopted broad-based categorical eligibility (BBCE), which raises the SNAP gross-income threshold from 130% to 200% of total household gross monthly income and removes asset limits for some households.
- **Advocacy group table (updated May 28, 2026):** It keeps the net income limit at 100% of the poverty line and lists monthly gross limits of $2,608 for one person and $5,358 for four. It also states that families previously denied for having more than $3,000 in savings should reapply (Raises gross income limit to 200% of the Federal Poverty Line (FPL) and maintains net income limit at 100% FPL).
- **Older Tennessee-specific guidance (January 2026):** This still shows the 130% gross limit, with the BBCE change described as pending legislative approval. It lists a $3,483 gross limit for a family of four, a $2,680 net limit, and asset limits of $3,000 (or $4,500 for households with a disabled or 60+ member) (The state is changing its BBCE rules, pending approval from the Tennessee General Assembly, which would simplify and align SNAP income limits with TANF.).
- **Federal FY2026 standards (October 2025 to September 2026):** One person has a $1,696 gross limit and $1,305 net limit; four people have $3,483 gross and $2,680 net. Tennessee follows the standard federal income test (the same limits used nationwide, except Alaska, Hawaii, and territories).
- **Exemptions:** Households with an elderly (60+) or disabled member only need to meet the net income test (Elderly or disabled households only need to meet the net income test.).
- **Conflicting figure:** One calculator site lists a four-person gross limit of $3,575 at 130% of the poverty line, which doesn't match the federal $3,483 figure. Treat it with caution.

Bottom line: the $3,483 (four-person) and $1,696 (one-person) figures are the federal FY2026 baseline. The 200% figures appear in more recent state-related materials, but I couldn't confirm an official TDHS announcement, so verify on TDHS's SNAP page or with 211 before relying on them.

The search didn't turn up Tennessee's October 2026 heating/cooling standard utility allowance (SUA) dollar amount, so I can't confirm that figure.

- **Tennessee's approach:** One source says Tennessee uses a standard utility allowance so households don't have to document each utility bill, and a set allowance is applied to the shelter calculation when heating or cooling costs are paid. The amount varies by household size.
- **Federal rule behind it:** FNS's final rule, effective January 17, 2025, gave state agencies until October 1, 2025 to ensure SUA values comply with the new methodology requirements. Under the methodology, the largest standard, the heating and cooling standard utility allowance, is set at the 80th percentile of low-income households' utility costs in the state. These figures are updated annually.
- **Pending legislation:** A 2026 bill, the Affordable Food and Energy Act, would let households use a state's heating-and-cooling SUA if they received more than $20 in LIHEAP or similar energy help in the current month or the past 12 months, if the state chooses that SUA. I found no evidence it has been enacted.

For the exact October 2026 Tennessee figures, check the Tennessee Department of Human Services SNAP page or the USDA FNS state SUA tables directly.

The FY 2027 maximum excess shelter deduction for the 48 states and D.C. is **$769**, up from $744 in FY 2026. The USDA's own FY 2027 COLA memo, effective October 1, 2026, sets the 48-state figure at $769, and several secondary sources match it.

- **Primary source:** The USDA memo covers the 48 contiguous states, D.C., Alaska, Guam, Hawaii, and the U.S. Virgin Islands, and it sets the shelter cap at $769 for the 48 states and D.C. The shelter cap value will increase to $769 for the 48 States and D.C.
- **Prior year:** A comparison table lists the FY 2026 figure at $744, so the change is $25. Maximum excess shelter deduction (48 states and D.C.) | $744 | $769
- **Territories and other areas:** Alaska's cap is $1,229, Guam's is $903, Hawaii's is $1,036, and the Virgin Islands' is $606. Maximum excess shelter deductions: 48 states and D.C.: $769 (up from $744)
- **Exception:** One source says the cap does not apply to households with an elderly or disabled member. The $769 cap does not apply to households with an elderly or disabled member.

The USDA memo is the authoritative source. The other results are secondary outlets, and they agree with it on the $769 figure.

Thanks. $300 in savings is well under the older $3,000 limit I found, so savings shouldn't get in your way.

**Where you stand: possibly.**
- **Income after deductions:** It looks like you'd pass. Your adjusted income is about $1,199, and the limit is $1,330.
- **Income before deductions:** This is still the one open question. You're at $1,770, which is $41 over the 130% limit of $1,729 ([News4Jax, reporting USDA's FY2027 numbers](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)). If Tennessee uses the reported 200% limit, you'd pass. I couldn't confirm that on an official page.
- **Estimated benefit:** About $25 to $150 a month. This is a rough estimate. Tennessee's exact utility allowance would narrow it.

**What I'd do next**
1. Apply online at the [One DHS Customer Portal](https://onedhs.tn.gov/csp). You can also call 1-833-772-8347 (TTY 711), per [TDHS](https://www.tn.gov/humanservices/for-families/supplemental-nutrition-assistance-program-snap.html).
2. Have your recent pay stubs, your lease, and an electric bill handy.
3. If you want help with the application, call 211 for free local help.

Applying costs nothing. A caseworker will check the current income limit and work rules, and only TDHS can decide.

Please report your income and rent exactly as they are. That protects you from having to pay back an overpayment later.

Do you want me to check whether you might also qualify for health coverage through TennCare?

Sources:
- [News4Jax: SNAP benefits increase](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)
